learn.hook: For over a century, Newton's particle picture of light ruled. Then a thin film of soap and two tiny slits showed that light behaves like waves.
points: Newton favoured a corpuscular (particle) model of light. Huygens (1678) proposed a wave model.

Young's interference experiment (1801) and later Maxwell's electromagnetic theory established the wave nature of light. The wave model also correctly predicts that light travels slower in water than in air.
Ray optics is the limit of wave optics when the wavelength is very small compared with the size of obstacles and apertures.
A wavefront is a surface of constant phase. A point source gives spherical wavefronts; a line source gives cylindrical ones; far from any source, small portions are plane wavefronts.
Rays are perpendicular to wavefronts, and energy travels along the rays, perpendicular to the wavefront.

example.q: What shape of wavefront reaches Earth from a distant star, and why?
steps: A star is a point source, so its wavefronts are spherical.
Its distance is enormous, so the sphere's radius is huge.
A small part of a huge sphere is practically flat.

learn.reallife: The rainbow colours you see in a soap bubble or an oil film on a wet Mumbai road during the monsoon are evidence of light's wave nature through interference.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What exactly is a wavefront?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A wavefront is a surface of constant phase, and the rays are perpendicular to it. Wave-tastic!
teach.nudge: Good! What is the same at every point on a wavefront?

revise.summary: Newton favoured particles, but Huygens proposed waves, and Young's interference (1801) and Maxwell's theory established light as a wave. A wavefront is a surface of constant phase, spherical near a point source and plane far away, with rays perpendicular to it.
remember: Point source → spherical; line source → cylindrical; distant → plane
Rays ⟂ wavefronts; light slower in water
traps: Huygens, not Newton, proposed the wave theory
Energy flows perpendicular to, not along, wavefronts

learn.hook: Drop pebbles in a still pond: each ripple spreads in circles. Huygens imagined every point on a wave doing exactly that.
points: Huygens principle: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets that spread out at the wave speed. The new wavefront is the forward envelope (common tangent) of these wavelets.
The backward wave is ignored; a fuller theory shows that the amplitude of the backwave is zero, so the wave only goes forward.
Reflection by Huygens construction: comparing two triangles formed by the incident and reflected wavefronts proves that i = r.

Wavefronts through optical elements: a plane wave through a thin prism is tilted; through a convex lens it becomes a converging spherical wave; after reflection from a concave mirror it becomes a spherical wave converging to the focus.
Optical paths: all rays from a point to its image take the same time (equal optical path), which is why lenses work.

example.q: Explain using Huygens principle why a plane wave stays plane as it travels in a uniform medium.
steps: Each point on the plane wavefront sends out spherical wavelets.
After time t, all have radius vt.
Their forward common tangent is a plane parallel to the original.
example.answer: The envelope of equal wavelets is a parallel plane, so the wave stays plane

learn.reallife: Ultrasound scanners in Indian hospitals shape their beams using arrays of tiny sources, an engineering application of Huygens' idea that a wavefront is built from many secondary wavelets.

So they travel at the same speed as the wave
Answer: the same speed as the original wave

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A lens forms an image because all rays from an object point reach the image point in equal times. Reason (R): Light travels slower in glass, so the thicker central part of a convex lens delays the central rays. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false

quiz.explain: Extra glass in the middle compensates for the shorter geometrical path, equalising travel times.
steps: A: rays from an object point reach the image in equal times – true
R: thicker glass at the centre delays central rays – true
The delay equalises travel times, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not see the role of delay in glass

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How did Huygens explain how a wave moves forward?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Every point on a wavefront sends out secondary wavelets; their forward envelope is the new wavefront. Ripple power!
teach.nudge: Good! What does each point on a wavefront do in Huygens' picture?

revise.summary: Huygens principle: each point of a wavefront emits secondary wavelets and the new wavefront is their forward envelope. It explains reflection (i = r) and how prisms, lenses and mirrors reshape wavefronts.
remember: New wavefront = forward envelope of wavelets
Convex lens / concave mirror: plane → converging spherical
traps: Secondary wavelets do not travel faster or slower; they move at the same speed as the wave
Image formation needs equal optical paths, not equal geometric paths

learn.hook: Imagine a marching band walking from a road onto sand at an angle. The band members who hit the sand first slow down, and the whole row turns. Light does the same.
points: Huygens construction for refraction: while one end of the wavefront travels v₁τ in medium 1, the wavelet from the other end travels v₂τ in medium 2. Comparing triangles gives sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁ (Snell's law).
Entering a denser medium (v₂ < v₁): the ray bends towards the normal.
Frequency stays the same across the boundary; speed and wavelength change: λ₂/λ₁ = v₂/v₁, so λ in medium = λ₀/n.
Going into a rarer medium (v₂ > v₁): the ray bends away from the normal. When sin i = v₁/v₂, r = 90°; beyond this critical angle, no refracted wavefront forms, giving total internal reflection.
Example: in glass of n = 1.5, light of vacuum wavelength 600 nm has λ = 400 nm and speed 2 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

example.q: Yellow light of wavelength 589 nm in air enters water (n = 1.33). Find its frequency, speed and wavelength in water.

learn.reallife: Fishermen in Kerala aim their spears below where a fish appears, because light from the fish refracts at the water surface, bending as its speed changes.

revise.summary: Huygens construction gives Snell's law: sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁. Frequency stays the same while speed and wavelength drop by n in a denser medium, and beyond the critical angle no refracted wave forms.
focus: Changes in v, λ and ν
remember: ν unchanged; λ = λ₀/n; v = c/n
traps: Frequency does not change on refraction
Wavelength decreases, not increases, in a denser medium

learn.hook: Two speakers playing the same note can make spots of silence in a room. Light waves can do the same, if their sources are perfectly in step.
points: Coherent sources keep a constant phase difference; incoherent sources have a phase difference that changes randomly and rapidly.
Two coherent waves of equal intensity I₀ meeting with phase difference φ give resultant intensity I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2).
Constructive interference (bright, I = 4I₀) for path difference nλ (φ = 2nπ); destructive (dark, I = 0) for path difference (n + ½)λ (φ = (2n + 1)π).
For incoherent sources, the cos² term averages to ½, so the intensities simply add: I = 2I₀. No fringes are seen.
Interference can be demonstrated with water waves: two dippers moving up and down together in a ripple tank produce lines of calm and agitated water.

example.q: Two coherent waves of intensity I₀ each meet with a path difference of λ/3. Find the resultant intensity.

learn.reallife: Noise-cancelling headphones sold across India work by destructive interference: they produce sound waves that cancel incoming noise.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why don't two torches shining together make bright and dark stripes?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Two torches are incoherent: their phase difference changes randomly, so the pattern washes out. Need coherent sources!
teach.nudge: Good! What must be true of two sources to give a steady interference pattern?

revise.summary: Coherent sources keep a constant phase difference. Two coherent waves of intensity I₀ give I = 4I₀cos²(φ/2): bright for path difference nλ and dark for (n + ½)λ; incoherent sources just add to 2I₀.
remember: Bright: Δ = nλ (I = 4I₀); dark: Δ = (n + ½)λ (I = 0)
traps: Independent lamps cannot give steady fringes
Energy is redistributed, not destroyed, in interference

learn.hook: Thomas Young needed two light sources perfectly in step. His trick was simple and brilliant: split the light from one source using two pinholes.
points: Two independent sources are incoherent. Young used light from a single source passing through two narrow slits S₁ and S₂, which then act as coherent sources.
For slits separated by d, screen at distance D (D ≫ d), the path difference at a point at height x on the screen is S₂P - S₁P ≈ xd/D.
Bright fringes at x = nλD/d (n = 0, ±1, ±2...); dark fringes at x = (n + ½)λD/d.
Fringe width (distance between consecutive bright or dark fringes): β = λD/d. The fringes are equally spaced.
The central fringe (x = 0, zero path difference) is always bright.

example.q: In a YDSE, d = 1 mm, D = 1 m and λ = 600 nm. Find the fringe width and the position of the third bright fringe.
example.answer: β = 0.6 mm; third bright fringe at 1.8 mm

learn.reallife: Physics students in Indian colleges measure the wavelength of sodium light using double-slit or biprism set-ups, with fringe widths measured to a hundredth of a millimetre.

teach.nudge: Good! What decides whether a point on the screen is bright or dark?

revise.summary: In Young's experiment two slits lit by one source act as coherent sources. At height x the path difference is xd/D, so bright fringes lie at nλD/d and dark fringes at (n + ½)λD/d, with equal fringe width β = λD/d.
remember: Bright: x = nλD/d; dark: x = (n + ½)λD/d
traps: The 2nd dark fringe is at 1.5β, not 2β
Don't substitute nm or mm directly; convert to metres

learn.hook: Swap red light for blue, dunk the apparatus in water, or move the screen back: each tweak stretches or squeezes the fringes in a predictable way.
points: β = λD/d: β increases with λ and D, and decreases with d.
Immersing the apparatus in a liquid of refractive index n reduces λ to λ/n, so β becomes β/n.
With white light, the central fringe is white, and the others are coloured: violet (shorter λ) fringes lie nearer the centre, red ones farther out. Only a few fringes are visible.
Energy is redistributed in interference: it is not destroyed at dark fringes but moved to bright ones.
Fringe shift problems: λ can be found from measured fringe width or from the change in position of a given fringe when D or λ changes.

example.q: Fringes of width 0.6 mm are formed in air. Find the fringe width when the whole apparatus is immersed in water (n = 4/3).

learn.reallife: Engineers at ISRO use interferometers, which measure tiny distances by counting fringe shifts, to test the flatness of mirrors and lenses for satellite cameras.

learn.hook: Look at a street light through a narrow gap between two fingers on a dark night. You will see faint bright and dark bands: light bending round the edges.
points: Diffraction is the bending of light around the edges of obstacles or apertures whose size is comparable to the wavelength.
A single slit of width a gives a broad central maximum with weaker secondary maxima and minima on either side.
Minima occur at a sinθ = nλ (n = ±1, ±2, ...); secondary maxima lie roughly at θ ≈ (n + ½)λ/a, with intensity falling quickly.
Angular width of the central maximum = 2λ/a; on a screen at distance D its linear width = 2λD/a. The central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum.
Narrower slits give wider diffraction patterns.

example.q: Light of 600 nm falls on a slit of width 0.2 mm. Find the width of the central maximum on a screen 1 m away.

learn.reallife: The coloured patterns you see in the tiny tracks of a CD or DVD lying in an Indian home, or in a peacock's feathers, involve diffraction and interference of light.

quiz.q: Why do we hear sound around corners but cannot see around them?
options: Sound wavelengths (metres) are comparable to doorways; light wavelengths (~500 nm) are far smaller
Our eyes are blocked by walls but ears are not

steps: Sound λ (metres) ≈ doorway size, so it diffracts strongly
Light λ (~500 nm) is far smaller, so it barely bends
Answer: Sound wavelengths (metres) are comparable to doorways; light wavelengths (~500 nm) are far smaller

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does light spread out after going through a very narrow slit?'
teach.praise: Chirp! When the slit is comparable to the wavelength, light diffracts, bending and spreading out; narrower slit, wider pattern!
teach.nudge: Good! What effect is this, and when is it noticeable?

revise.summary: Diffraction is the bending of light around apertures comparable to its wavelength. A single slit of width a gives a broad central maximum with minima at a sinθ = nλ; the central width is 2λ/a in angle or 2λD/a on a screen.
traps: First minimum is at a sinθ = λ, not λ/2
The central width does not grow with slit width; it is ∝ 1/a

learn.hook: Both interference and diffraction give bright and dark bands. A careful look at the band widths and brightness tells you which one you are seeing.
points: Interference (two slits): fringes of equal width β = λD/d and (ideally) equal intensity.
Diffraction (single slit): a central maximum twice as wide as the others, with intensity falling rapidly for higher orders.
Interference comes from superposition of waves from two separate (coherent) sources; diffraction from superposition of wavelets from different parts of one wavefront.

Activity: hold two razor blades edge to edge to form a narrow slit and look at a distant frosted bulb with a straight filament; you see a diffraction pattern. Safety: handle blades carefully, with edges away from fingers, and never look at the Sun.
In a real double-slit experiment, each slit's diffraction pattern acts as an envelope over the interference fringes.

example.q: A pattern shows bands of equal width and equal brightness. Is it interference or single-slit diffraction?
steps: Single-slit diffraction has a central band twice as wide as the rest.
Diffraction bands fade quickly away from the centre.
Equal widths and brightness match two-source interference.

learn.reallife: The colourful bands you see when looking at a bright street lamp through a fine cotton dupatta or umbrella fabric are diffraction patterns from the tiny gaps between threads.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Both interference and diffraction make stripes. How can I tell them apart?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Interference fringes are equal in width and brightness; diffraction has a central band twice as wide and the rest fade fast. Spotted!
teach.nudge: Good! Compare the widths and brightness of the bands in each pattern.

revise.summary: Interference from two coherent sources gives equally spaced, equally bright fringes; single-slit diffraction gives a central maximum twice as wide as others with fading intensity, from wavelets of one wavefront. In real double slits, diffraction envelopes the fringes.
traps: Don't confuse slit separation d with slit width a
Never look at the Sun through slits

learn.hook: Tilt your head while wearing polarising sunglasses and look at an LCD screen: it can go dark. Light has a hidden direction, and polaroids can reveal it.
points: Polarisation shows that light is a transverse wave. Analogy: a wave on a string passes through a vertical slit only if the string vibrates vertically.
Unpolarised light (sunlight, bulbs) has its electric field vibrating in all directions perpendicular to the direction of travel, changing randomly.
Plane (linearly) polarised light has its electric field vibrating in one direction only.
A polaroid transmits only the component of E along its pass axis. Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ through one polaroid becomes polarised with intensity I₀/2, whatever the polaroid's orientation.
A second polaroid (the analyser) rotated in front of the first changes the intensity: maximum when the axes are parallel, zero when crossed.

example.q: Unpolarised light of intensity 80 W m⁻² passes through a polaroid. What is the transmitted intensity, and does it change if the polaroid is rotated?
steps: A polaroid transmits half of unpolarised light.
Rotating it does not change this, because unpolarised light has no preferred direction.

learn.reallife: Polarising sunglasses popular with drivers on Indian highways cut glare from wet roads and car bonnets, because the reflected glare is partly polarised.

items: Polarisation proves that light is a transverse wave.

Sound waves in air can be polarised.

I = I₀/2.
Rotating a single polaroid in unpolarised light makes the light flicker.
Transmitted intensity stays I₀/2.
Two crossed polaroids block the light completely.
The second removes the remaining component.

quiz.explain: Unpolarised light has no preferred direction.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Light passing through a polaroid has half the intensity of the incident unpolarised light. Reason (R): The polaroid passes only the component of E along its axis, and averaging over all directions gives one half. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: The average of cos²θ over all angles is ½.
steps: A: a polaroid halves unpolarised intensity – true
R: it passes the E component along its axis; average of cos²θ is ½ – true
R gives the ½, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not see why exactly half passes

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What does a polaroid do to ordinary sunlight?'
teach.praise: Chirp! It lets through only the E vibrations along its axis, so the light becomes polarised at half intensity. Proof that light is transverse!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to the intensity, and what is special about the light that comes out?

revise.summary: Polarisation shows light is a transverse wave. Unpolarised light has E in all perpendicular directions; a polaroid passes only the component along its axis, giving plane polarised light of half the intensity, and crossed polaroids block it.
remember: One polaroid: I = I₀/2 for unpolarised light
Only transverse waves can be polarised
traps: Rotating one polaroid in unpolarised light does not change the intensity
Sound in air cannot be polarised

topics.title: Malus' law and uses of polaroids

learn.hook: 3D movies in Indian multiplexes send two polarised images at once, one for each eye. Your 3D glasses use polaroids to separate them.
points: Malus' law: when plane polarised light of intensity I₀ falls on an analyser whose axis makes angle θ with the polarisation, the transmitted intensity is I = I₀ cos²θ.
θ = 0: full transmission; θ = 90°: zero; θ = 45°: I₀/2; θ = 60°: I₀/4.
Three polaroids: unpolarised I₀ → first polaroid → I₀/2, then multiply by cos² of each successive angle between axes.
Two crossed polaroids block all light, but inserting a third polaroid at 45° between them lets I₀/8 through.
Uses: sunglasses (cut glare), camera filters, LCD screens of phones and calculators, and 3D movie glasses.

example.q: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through three polaroids. The second is at 45° to the first, and the third is at 90° to the first. Find the final intensity.
steps: After P₃ (45° to P₂): I₀/4 × cos²45° = I₀/8

learn.reallife: Calculator and digital watch displays made for Indian classrooms use liquid crystals between polarisers; applying a voltage rotates the light's polarisation and darkens the digits.

quiz.explain: After the first: 16. After the second: 16 × cos²45° = 8.

quiz.q: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through three polaroids: P₁, P₂ at 30° to P₁, and P₃ at 90° to P₁. What is the final intensity (as a fraction of I₀)?
quiz.mistake: Thinks crossed first and third polaroids always block light

quiz.q: Two polaroids are crossed. A third polaroid is inserted between them with its axis at 45°. What fraction of unpolarised light now passes?
quiz.explain: I₀/2 × ½ × ½ = I₀/8.
steps: After 45° polaroid: × ½ ⇒ I₀/4; after the last (45° more): × ½
quiz.mistake: Thinks crossed polaroids always give zero

quiz.q: Why do polarising sunglasses reduce glare from a wet road?
options: They are darker than ordinary glass
Light reflected from the road is partly polarised, and the lenses block that polarisation
quiz.explain: Reflected glare is largely horizontally polarised; the lenses' axis is vertical.
steps: Light reflected from a wet road is partly polarised
Polaroid lenses block that polarisation, cutting glare
Answer: Light reflected from the road is partly polarised, and the lenses block that polarisation
quiz.mistake: Thinks they are just tinted glass

quiz.q: At what angle should an analyser be set relative to the polariser to transmit half of the polarised light (in degrees)?
quiz.explain: cos²45° = ½.
quiz.mistake: Uses 60°, where cos = ½ but cos² = ¼

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If I turn a polaroid in front of polarised light, how much light gets through?'
teach.praise: Chirp! By Malus' law, I = I₀ cos²θ: full at 0°, half at 45°, none at 90°. Spin to dim!
teach.nudge: Good! Which law gives the intensity, and how does it depend on the angle?

revise.summary: Malus' law gives I = I₀cos²θ for polarised light through an analyser at angle θ. With several polaroids, halve the unpolarised intensity once and then multiply by cos² of each successive angle; polaroids are used in sunglasses, cameras, LCDs and 3D glasses.
remember: Third polaroid at 45° between crossed ones → I₀/8
traps: Don't halve at every polaroid; halve only once, for the first polaroid on unpolarised light
Don't use each polaroid's angle to the first; use the angle between successive polaroids
